Introduction

Welcome to the first blog in a series where I'll try my best to close up some of the functionality gabs between the old SAP BW system and  SAP Datasphere.
With the end of life for the old SAP BW systems in sight, companies and developers have been diving deep into SAP Datasphere, to build new, exciting solutions, in addition to migrating existing reports. 

Personally, I've been involved with several Datasphere implementations now, and one thing I have found myself missing a lot was the standard Exit variables for things like "Current month", "Current year" and so on. 

To make my life, and hopefully yours as well, I've recreated a set of the old date / calendar variables.
All the views are bundled in a nice package, which you can download from this GitHub repo. 

How to install:

Note: Your Datasphere tenant does not need to be connected to the Content Network for this to work. 

One the package is installed, you may, or may not, need to change the source of the view 2VR_CALENDER_WRAPPER, which is the basis of all the other views. 
This was simply done to make sure that even if your space does not contain the Time Objects, you only have to remap 1 object. 

  1. Go to this GitHub Repo and download the package
  2. Go to your Datasphere tenant and select "Import":
  3. Click Upload and select the package downloaded in step 1.
  4. After the import is complete click the package:
  5. Under "Import Options", map the space:

     

  6. And click "Import". 
  7. (Certain cases): If the view "SAP.TIME.VIEW_DIMENSION_DAY" is not present in the target space open the view 2VR_CALENDER_WRAPPER and replace the source.

 

How were they implemented:

All the views are implemented as SQL views, and only return a single column, depending on the kind of view, rather than an interval, which some SAP BW variables might give. The reason for that is explained in the example below. 

All views have an input parameter, IP_OFFSET, which takes an integer, and will offset the result by one "unit" of time. 
So the CALYEAR views will offset one year at a time, the month views will offset one month at the time, and so on. 

Example: Analytical Models

In Datasphere, an Analytical Model is the final (kind of, that's not important now) step in the data modelling process. 
In your analytical model, you can define different kind of variables, that allows you to derive a value from a view, or a dynamic default. 
Note:  Deriving select options and intervals are not supported. 

In the above example, the user will be prompted to fill in an interval, but will only derive the first value:

If you want an interval, you'll need "Multiple single values".

In the above example, we've provided a view that returns three values, which will act as an interval.
Note: We have also provided the value -1 for the offset.

Which means all the values, 202601, 202512, 202511, and 202510 is offset by -1:

Implemented Variables

I've created variables for the following date objects:

  • 0CALDAY: Date (YYYYMMDD)
  • 0CALMONTH: Cal. Year / Month (YYYYMM)
  • 0CALQUARTER: Cal. Year / Quarter (YYYYQ)
  • 0CALWEEK: Cal. Year / Week (YYYYWW)
  • 0CALYEAR: Calendar Year (YYYY)

Because - well, because those were the ones that had been giving me headaches.

entry.title: BW Modernisation with the SAP BW Data Product Generator
entry.content:
The DataProduct Generator for SAP Business Data Cloud in SAP BW/4HANA Administration Cockpit

With the "SAP BW/4HANA DataProduct Generator for SAP BDC" a functionality is availabe as part of the BW/4HANA Administration Cockpit to expose existing SAP BW/4HANA artifacts ( i.e. Advanced DataStore Objects, CompositeProviders and Queries as an InfoProvider) as local tables to the Object Store. For SAP BW 7.5 there is a SAP GUI based UI available. In a second step the Data Sharing Cockpit of Datasphere can be used to create DataProducts out of such local tables.

1) Activities in the Data Provisioning Cockpit:

Scenario: The underlying Scenario of this chapter is to create a DataProduct out of an Advanced DataStore Object from a SAP BW/4HANA system in the private Cloud which containes additional CashFlow data. This data should be made available as a DataProduct to BDC to be merged with the existing Working Capital data from the exercises before.

Update March 2026: Since the availability of SAP BW/4HANA Modeling Tools in Eclipse 1.27 there is an additional way to move a BW/4HANA InfoProvider to the Object Store of SAP Datasphere (as a basis for the Data Product generation). As a result, a subscription is generated. A data subscription is a new BW object type that allows you to extract data from ODP-based sources within your BW system into local tables (file) in the SAP Datasphere system of your SAP Business Data Cloud formation. In the following chapters both options are described:

1.1) Exposing an InfoProvider of SAP BW/4HANA via the Data Product Generator (in SAP BW/4HANA Administration Cockpit)

  • Establish a subscription in SAP BW/4HANA Administration Cockpit, select the InfoProvider which needs to be exposed to the ObjectStore and activate the subscription:

(remark: "CF in thge description of the objects in the screenshots is referring to the scenario of the exercise and means "Cash Flow")

  • Regular transfers can be scheduled from the subscription using a BW Process Chain. With every execution of the BW Process Chain the data is pushed into the SAP Datasphere object store. There is a new Process Type available to be used to propagate the data of an InfoProvider to the ObjectStore "Load Process and Postprocessing - Data Subscription":

The status of the latest execution of a subscription can be checked in the subscription overview:

For each subscription the local table can be viewed as well as its content. By pressing "View Local Table" for a given subscription you will be guided to the Datasphere instance and the respective local table in the Data Builder. From here the content of the table can also be checked.

1.2) Exposing an InfoProvider of SAP BW/4HANA via the Scenario Generator (with the SAP BW/4HANA Modeling Tools in Eclipse)

With the SAP BW/4HANA Modelling Tools in Eclipse 1.27 there is an additional possibility to expose a BW InfoProvider to the Object Store of SAP Datasphere. Eitherway, regardless which option is used, the local table (subscription) has to be used as a basis in the Data Sharing Cockpit to generate a Data Product.

There are three important concepts which neeed to be considered using the Scenario Generator:

A 'scenario' is a list of references between data subscriptions which are required to reconstruct a specific BW model (such as a DataStore object (advanced) (aDSO) or a CompositeProvider (HCPR)). For example, if you have a CompositeProvider, you would not only need a data subscription to represent the top-level object, but also further data subscriptions for the InfoObjects it contains and other dependencies.

The 'scenario tree' saves these dependencies between the objects in the BW model, as well as the equivalent data subscriptions and their dependencies. It also considers existing data subscriptions for dependent objects to avoid the creation of duplicate data subscriptions and local tables (file).

The 'Scenario Generator' lets you not only create scenarios out of your BW models, but also mass generate the associated data subscriptions out of the scenario tree. Through this you can replicate an entire BW model into local tables (file) in your SAP Datasphere tenant in SAP Business Data Cloud. There, the extracted data and associated semantics are stored in table format and become available for further use cases, such as creating data products or sharing to SAP Databricks.

So the basic workflow in the Scenario Generator is:

a) To create a Scenario which is a collection of all Objects belonging to a given BW InfoProvider and their dependencies. For example a CompositeProvider alone does not contain any data. The data is coming from its PartProviders so a scenario of a CompositeProvider would also include the PartProviders.

b) Generate the subscriptions which consists of the lokal tables and the mechanisms to replicate the data from the InfoProviders to the local tables

As a basis for the Data Product to be created this time the CompositeProvider (DPG_CP_CF) from the scenario above is taken. In the Scenario Generators first tab 'Scenario Core Objects' some general settings can be made before collecting the objects related to a selected InfoProvider to create the scenario and the dependency tree of all objects belonging to the scenario.

  • 'Selection Grouping' defines which related objects shoud be collected for a selected BW InfoProvider. It can be specified that 'only necessary' objects are taken into consideration or also the Upstream and downstream objects along the Dataflow of the InfoProvider.
  • The 'Association Levels' define the amount of levels included in the dependency tree.
  • There are some optional checkboxes to activate the possibility to transport subscriptions or to consider already existing subscriptions to prevent duplicates and redundant subscriptions on objects where a subscription already exists.

After pressing the 'Collect' Button, all dependent objects from the CompositeProvider are collected which are the Inbound ADSO as the only PartProvider and the second Object collected is the InfoObject 'Company Code' which is the only real InfoObject in the Inbound ADSO (rest of the columns are fieldbased).

After the collection of the objects the relationsships are displayed in the Tab 'Object Relations'. In this list all subscriptions which are generated in this second step can be seen and the generation of the subscription triggered. After this the 'Message' tab is shown where all relevant messages from the generation process can be seen.

2) Creation of a DataProduct out of the exposed SAP BW/4HANA ADSO

To create a DataProduct from the local table the Data Sharing Studio from Datasphere must be used. In a BDC Formation there can only be one Datasphere System assigned to the BW 7.5 or BW/4HANA instance.

Before the DataProduct can be generated, a Data Provider Profile must be defined (or an existing one used) where the mandatory flag "Data Provider Visibility" is set to "Unified Customer Landscape Formations".

Now a new DataProduct can be created (Data Sharing Cockpit > My Data Products > Create Product)

In the definition of the DataProduct the fields for the Contexts and Deliverymode are automatically taken from the Data Provider Profile and to connect to the right ADSO the corresponding Datasphere Space needs to be specified where the ADSO is located:

After saving the DataProduct it should be available in the overview table under "My Data Products". By selecting this entry in the table the Status can be switched to "listed".

3) Next Steps

Create a graphical view to bring the data of this newly created DataProduct together to share it with other data in SAP Datasphere or expose the Data Product for further Analytical Scenarios (e.g. via Databricks).

 

4) Important Links / Notes

Pre-requisites

  • SAP Note [3590400 - Configuration SAP BW and SAP BW/4HANA: Data Product Generator for SAP Business Data Cloud] (https://me.sap.com/notes/3590400)

  • SAP Note [3590318 Pilot BW Configuration for Data Product Generator in SAP BDC] (https://me.sap.com/notes/3590318)

  • SAP Note [3593519, TCI2 for BW on HANA, BW/4HANA] (https://me.sap.com/notes/3593519)

  • SAP Note 3581186 - OA2C: RFC API

  • SAP Notes for Transaction SOAUTH2_CLIENT:

  • 3532137 - OA2C: Dynpro UI for OAuth2.0 Client Configuration

  • 3561719 - OA2C: New dynpro UI SOAUTH2_CLIENT, generation of DDIC object

  • 3561640 - OA2C: Token Status for SOAUTH2_CLIENT

  • 3692414 - Data Subscription TLOGO: After TCI 3.0

  • Supported Releases of SAP BW 7.5 / SAP BW/4HANA:

  • SAP BW 7.50 SP24 onwards

  • SAP BW/4HANA 2021 SP4 onwards

  • SAP BW/4HANA 2023 SP0 onwards

entry.title: BI Remediation Checks during ECC to S/4HANA Migration
entry.content:
As SAP prepares to end support for ECC by 2027, many organizations are making the crucial move to SAP S/4HANA. The shift can unlock improved capabilities and performance, but it can also introduce changes that ripple through the BI landscape if we don’t plan for them early.

From a BI perspective, there are multiple aspects to consider during the transition. This blog focuses on the BI remediation checks that help protect data trust, reporting, and decision-making continuity during and after the migration.

Why do we need BI remediation? 
The migration from SAP ECC to SAP S/4HANA introduces significant changes to the underlying data structures. These changes impact how data is extracted, modelled, and consumed in the BI system. Because of that, reporting remediation becomes critical to ensure data consistency, accuracy, and continuity in analytics after the migration.

With remediation, we ensure:

  • BI models and reports remain functional and aligned with the new S/4HANA structures
  • Disruption is minimized for business operations and reporting processes

Data model simplifications in S/4HANA (what changes underneath)
When SAP S/4HANA was first introduced, the SAP ERP 6.0 data model underwent major restructuring. Redundancies were removed, and many smaller tables were consolidated into fewer, larger ones.
Figure 1 can help visualize the concept and why “what worked in ECC” may not behave the same way in S/4HANA.

                                                                                                 FIGURE 1

Impact of S/4HANA migration on the BI system (what to check)

1) Impact on BW Datasources / Extractors
If you run SAP BW, one of the first questions is:
“After ECC becomes S/4HANA, will my extractors and DataSources still be supported and behave the same way?”
SAP note 2500202  provides an Excel sheet produced by SAP that details the impact of S/4HANA on BW Datasources. This sheet is periodically updated. The same note also contains a PPT that guides us on how to interpret and use the Excel list.

A proven approach is:

  • Inventory your active extractors (e.g., via ROOSOURCE).  
  • Identify which are truly used (process chains / BI statistics where available)
  • Cross-check them against the SAP note 2500202 list and categorize outcomes (no change / restricted / obsolete / alternative required)

2) Tables with Replacement Objects (don’t rely on “classic tables” blindly)
If, as part of your BI remediation strategy, you plan to continue using certain classic ECC tables, for example, relying on MARD instead of adopting the newer MATDOC structure, you must depend on the corresponding Replacement Object rather than accessing the table directly.
With the data model simplification in SAP S/4HANA, many traditional ECC tables are no longer the authoritative “single source of truth.” In many cases, data is aggregated or derived via CDS views that join and enrich information from multiple sources. Because of this shift, it becomes essential to transition from reading classic tables (such as MARC, MARD, and others) to using their designated Replacement Objects, ensuring that analytics and integrations receive accurate, up‑to‑date data.

  • In Native HANA, it is advisable to verify whether a table has a replacement object or whether it can still be used directly.
  • In SAP BW, the datasource typically absorbs most of the underlying data model changes. However, in hybrid scenarios, particularly when calculation views are built on ECC base tables or when custom datasources built on ECC base tables, it becomes essential to thoroughly assess the impact on the affected tables.

Figure 2 shows an example for table MARD. NSDM_E_MARD serves as the replacement view for the classic MARD table. Although data continues to reside in MARD, those entries generally represent older documents migrated to S/4HANA or new S/4HANA records that are stored without measure fields. To obtain the full set of information (both characteristics and measures) for transactions created in S/4HANA, you must use the replacement object, in this case NSDM_E_MARD, rather than relying on MARD directly.

                                                                                                     FIGURE 2

3) Replacement of obsolete tables
Some ECC tables are replaced or made obsolete, and direct reporting on such tables is no longer recommended or supported. Examples tables include:

  • KONV, VBUP, VBUK, EIKP, EIPO

Obsolete tables may still exist, but they can behave as compatibility views. For accuracy and performance, they should be switched to transparent tables where applicable.

  • SAP Note 3250204: describes about the replacement table PRDC_ELEMENTS for KNOV table.
  • SAP Note 2198647: talks about tables VBUP, VBUK and SD data model changes.
  • SAP Note 3482527: covers about new S/4HANA foreign trade. 

4) Key fields changed (primary key shifts can break pipelines)
In S/4HANA, the primary keys of some tables have changed compared to ECC. Some examples are:

  • VBFA
  • FAAV_ANLC

These changes directly affect how data is stored, identified, and retrieved. That can break:

  • Joins in HANA models
  • Deduplication logic
  • Delta logic or key-based transformations in BW

Action

  • Review where these tables are used in extraction/transformation layers
  • Re-check join conditions, uniqueness assumptions, and surrogate key logic
  • Re-test deltas and aggregations end-to-end

5) Field length extensions (small change, big downstream effect)
Some fields were extended in S/4HANA to support broader functional requirements, enhanced integration needs, and future extensibility.
One such example is:

  • VBAP-VBTYP (Char1) Document Category replaced by VBAP-VBTYPL (Char4)
    • SAP Note 2495386 details the BW datasource that uses this object.

Another major example:

  • Material Number (SAP Note 2215424) changed from char(18) to char(40)

A key design decision regarding material numbers is whether your organization will:

  • Adopt a true 40‑character material number, introducing a new business meaning, or
  • Retain the existing 18‑character logic, while simply expanding the technical field length to 40 characters.

The chosen approach directly influences how material numbers flow through your BI data models and determines the adjustments required in downstream reporting and integrations.

6) Centralized Master Data via Business Partner (Customer/Vendor integration)
SAP fundamentally changed how master data is managed by introducing a unified, centralized model for customers, vendors, and business partners. This replaces the traditional ECC siloed structures with a harmonized object: the Business Partner (BP).
It’s not a “technical-only” change, it’s a semantic change in how master data is governed
Please check the SAP Note 2265093 note for more information.

7) Redirecting ECC Virtual Tables in HANA Calculation Views
When your BI models use calculation views that reference ECC base tables, these views must be updated after the migration to ensure they point to the corresponding objects in the S/4HANA system. Redirecting them is essential to prevent calculation view failures and to avoid inconsistent or incorrect analytical results after the migration. Please refer the blog for mitigation of this impact.

 
Final thoughts: ECC to S/4HANA migration is not only an ERP transformation, but also a BI continuity challenge. The safest approach is to treat BI remediation as a structured workstream, validating extractors, replacing obsolete dependencies, and proactively addressing table/key/field changes before they surface as production reporting issues.

If this post helps you structure your BI remediation checks, please consider sharing your own experiences or additions in the comments.

entry.title: Blog 3 - From BW 7.5 to SAP BDC: Reusing Extractors, Custom Logic, and Models Standard Extractors
entry.content:
This is part 3 of our blog series investigating how to reuse existing BW artefacts in BDC such as extractors and custom logic.

As organizations embrace cloud-native data architectures, the journey from SAP BW on HANA 7.5 to SAP Business Data Cloud (BDC) represents a critical modernization path. Our team recently completed a pilot implementation focusing on first, lifting BW into SAP BDC and modernizing it using SAP Datasphere as the primary target architecture.

This blog post shares practical insights and key learnings from this experience, particularly around handling standard extractors and preserving custom extractors business logic in SAP BDC.

I. The Challenge: Standard Extractors in a Modern Architecture

Think of standard SAP extractors as old filing systems that worked perfectly in traditional warehouses but struggle in modern cloud environments. Standard SAP extractors (2LIS_02_ITM, 0CO_OM_CCA_9, 2LIS_03_BF) present significant migration challenges when moving from traditional BW environments to SAP Business Data Cloud. This was primarily due to missing primary key definitions. SAP has modernized these extractors through SAP Datasphere, which acts as an intelligent intermediary that handles the complex transformation from legacy extraction patterns to cloud-native data products, enabling faster, more reliable data flows without requiring extensive custom coding.

Implementation Reality

With delta processing already active and productive in your Datasphere environment, the three critical extractors now operate seamlessly: 2LIS_02_ITM delivers purchase order changes, 0CO_OM_CCA_9 streams cost center postings, and 2LIS_03_BF provides material movements for non-cumulative inventory analysis. Datasphere eliminates traditional complexity by managing initialization, delta processing, and data semantics automatically, transforming raw SAP tables into business-ready entities (Purchase Orders, Cost Centers, Stock) that SAP Analytics Cloud can consume directly for analytics and planning scenarios. The same entities can also by consumed directly by SAP HANA Cloud for custom AI / ML scenarios or by end-to-end Intelligent Applications.

Design implications now that delta handling works

With delta mode active in Datasphere, your design simplifies and becomes more “cloud-native”:

  1. Each extractor follows a clear pattern:
  • Run initialization and delta in Replication Flow in Datasphere

 

  • Configure the extractor “primary key” in the Configure schema

 

  • Enable scheduled delta loads (e.g., hourly, daily, near real time).

 

  • New data is created in your source system (ECC or S4)

 

  • Deltas are replicated in Datasphere (table is filtered for the specific PO that was newly created)
  1. Operational benefits:
  • No more large daily full loads.
  • Network and storage usage is reduced because only changes move.
  • Latency improves: BDC can be updated much more frequently.
  • Monitoring focuses on delta queues and extractor status in Datasphere.

Practical checklist for your migration

When running this in a real project with delta fully available:

  • Per extractor:
    • Confirm that initialization has been done successfully in Datasphere.
    • Ensure delta jobs are configured, scheduled, and monitored.
    • Align delta frequency with business needs (close to real time vs batch).
  • In Datasphere:
    • Model business keys clearly (e.g., PO number, item, company code; Controlling area, cost center, period).
    • Build semantic models (views, business entities) that hide technical complexity from BDC consumers.Stay tuned for more details on this topic in the next blog post.
    • Use lineage so others know which extractors feed which BDC data products.
  • In BDC:
    • Point your analytical models and stories to the Datasphere-based artifacts instead of direct raw tables.
    • Design calculations assuming data is continuously refreshed via delta.

Beyond standard extractors, the real differentiation in a BDC migration comes from how you bring your custom fields and business logic in extractor enhancements into the new landscape.

 

II. How to Handle Custom Fields and Extractor Extensions in SAP Business Data Cloud, SAP Datasphere

Reusing a customer’s existing custom logic is essential in SAP because it preserves years of in-house business knowledge, avoids costly redevelopment, and accelerates modernization while keeping results from business outcomes without business disruption.

In our pilot, we showed how SAP Datasphere within SAP Business Data Cloud can consume SAP standard extractors enhanced by custom fields without redesigning the entire data flow from scratch. Using the 0FI_AP_4 extractor (which supports both full and delta loads) as an example, the steps below illustrate how to expose customized business rules in financial data end‑to‑end to BDC.

These steps are not meant to be a full tutorial on how to enhance a standard SAP extractor – that pattern has been around for decades – but we believe it is still useful to summarize the key activities here. We will also show how these enhanced extractors are replicated (initial load and delta) into SAP Datasphere, in SAP Business Data Cloud.

  1. Check Existing Fields and Enhancement Options
    1. In the source system, use RSA2 (or R0S2/RSA6 depending on release) to display DataSource 0FI_AP_4.
    2. Verify whether the fields you need are already present but hidden (this is common in standard extractors).
    3. If they are not available, plan to add them via an append structure and fill them using RSAP0001 or a BAdI implementation.
  2. Enhance the Extract Structure (Append Structure)
    1. Still in RSA2, navigate to the extract structure of 0FI_AP_4.
    2. Create an append structure and add your custom fields (usually prefixed with ZZ or YY).
    3. Assign correct data elements (taken from SE11 table definitions) and activate the append structure.

After activation, the new fields are physically part of the extract structure but not yet filled with data.

  1. Implement the Extractor Logic (User Exit / BAdI)
    1. Create or reuse an enhancement project in CMOD and assign enhancement RSAP0001.
    2. For transactional data, implement component EXIT_SAPLRSAP_001 (include ZXRSAU01) and write the ABAP logic that populates the new fields for DataSource 0FI_AP_4.
      • Use I_DATASOURCE in the exit to branch specifically on 0FI_AP_4.
      • Read the necessary tables (e.g. BSEG, BKPF or customer tables) with the SELECT statement and loop over the extraction internal table to fill the custom fields using field symbols.
    3. Activate the enhancement project and the include program.

(Alternative: in newer systems you can use the dedicated BAdI for DataSource enhancement instead of RSAP0001, the principle for the logic remains the same.)

  1. Unhide and Configure the Fields in RSA6
    1. Open RSA6 and choose the source system.
    2. Select DataSource 0FI_AP_4 in change mode.
    3. Locate the new fields and remove the Hide flag; if needed, adjust properties such as “field only known in exit”.
    4. Save and activate the DataSource so that the new fields become visible for extraction (RSA3) and for replication to BW/Datasphere.

If you extended an LO Cockpit DataSource, you might also need to check the extract structure and update/activate it via LBWE so that queue filling works correctly.

In our pilot, we have created a simple logic by assigning a single value (1000) to the controlling area.

  1. Replicate and Consume in SAP Datasphere within SAP BDC
    1. In SAP Datasphere, connect to the source system and activate the enhanced extractor 0FI_AP_4.
    2. Create a replication flow to run an initial full load and delta loads, now including the custom fields.
    3. Once the replication flow runs and creates the local table in Datasphere, the enhanced field has been replicated with its data automaticaly replicated.

This completes the chain from technical enhancement in S/4HANA (or ECC) to business‑ready data, analytics and AI in BDC, while following the standard BW enhancement process.

III. Next Steps: From data replication to answering business questions

Once extractors (standard and extended) are replicated into SAP Datasphere and exposed to BDC, the next step is to turn raw data into multi-dimensional models to provide data for analytical purposes to answer different business questions.

  1. In SAP Datasphere, build Analytic Models on top of the replicated tables and datasources, defining measures, dimensions and hierarchies that fulfill business requirements. The latest update on the data product generator allows to semantically import BW 7.5 PCE InfoProvider data (works like semantic onboarding but is triggered from BW side and pushed into the object store of SAP Datasphere).
  2. Publish these models as consumption artifacts (expose analytic models/views, create and share data products) that can be consumed by SAP Analytics Cloud , SAP HANA Cloud apps and other BDC clients, tools and applications.
  3. In SAP Analytics Cloud, create stories, dashboards, and planning models that leverage the Datasphere models for live reporting, seamless planning and simulation.
  4. In SAP HANA Cloud, build high performance end-to-end intelligent applications that leverage custom AI / ML and multi-model capabilities for structured and unstructured data.

This way, the project does not stop at data replication: it delivers an end‑to‑end analytical platform where business users consume trusted, delta‑enabled data products in SAP Business Data Cloud for fact based decision support.

Conclusion

Our pilot project demonstrated that migrating from SAP BW7.5 on HANA to SAP Business Data Cloud using SAP Datasphere is not only feasible but can be done while preserving critical business logic and custom investments.

The key to success lies in thorough planning, understanding the current state of your extraction landscape, and leveraging the migration as an opportunity to modernize while preserving what works. As SAP continues to enhance BDC capabilities, organizations can confidently plan their migration journeys knowing that both standard and custom extraction scenarios are well-supported.

Stay tuned for the 4th blog post in this series, ‘Beyond Data Warehousing, AI-assisted migration of Business Logic from BW 7.5 to BDC Part 1’

entry.title: The SAP BW Migration Decision: Your Real Options in 2026
entry.content:
The question most of the Clients with BW system are asking is What do we actually do about SAP BW?

This isn't a theoretical question anymore. BW 7.5 mainstream maintenance ends in 2027. Private Cloud Edition (PCE) extends that runway to 2030—but that's barely four years away, and four years moves fast when you're carrying years of accumulated business logic, custom transformations, and deeply embedded reporting dependencies. The pressure to act is real, and the cost of making the wrong call—getting trapped in a costly rework cycle or betting on a platform without a future—is significant.

What follows are the options being actively debated on the ground in 2026. Not vendor positioning. Not marketing decks. The actual trade-offs architects and platform owners are wrestling with.

Setting the Stakes: Why This Decision Is Harder Than It Looks

On the surface, "migrate off BW" sounds like a straightforward modernization exercise. In practice, it's one of the most consequential architectural decisions an SAP organization can make right now. The choice determines:

  • How much of your existing system logic can be used as-is versus needs to be rebuilt from scratch
  • How deeply your organization wants to leverage AI and cloud-native capabilities in future
  • Your Organization’s dependency on the SAP ecosystem versus willingness move beyond to operate across platforms
  • The total cost of system change over the next 5–10 years, not just the migration cost

Option 1 · SAP BW 7.5 PCE — The Stability Bridge

Overview

Lift your existing NetWeaver BW 7.5 environment into SAP's managed Private Cloud Edition, hosted in the Business Data Cloud (BDC). Models, logic, and processes are preserved. You get auto-patching and managed infrastructure without a significant architecture change.

Architecture

Option 1 · SAP BW 7.5 PCE  |  Maintenance to 2030

Sources feed unchanged BW 7.5 inside a SAP-managed private cloud boundary. Consumption via existing BO/SAC stack.

S/4HANA / ECC / Other sources → SAP BW 7.5 (unchanged) → Auto-patch · managed ops → SAC / BO reporting

Limitation: No new capabilities. Bridge to 2030, not a destination. Same decision awaits in 4 years.

 

The appeal

This is the lowest-disruption path. If your organization has deep BW investments—complex transformations, heavily customized InfoProviders, years of tuning—this option protects all of it while buying time. Maintenance is covered through 2030, and the operational burden shifts to SAP.

The reality check

You're essentially paying to extend a legacy architecture's life. There's no meaningful innovation on this path—no cloud-native scaling, no real AI/ML depth, no pathway to modern data product paradigms. When 2030 arrives, you'll face the same decision you're facing today, except with less time and potentially more technical debt. This is a bridge, not a destination.

Best suited for: Organizations under significant time or budget pressure that need to stabilize the platform and defer a larger transformation decision—while using the time window deliberately to plan a real migration.

Option 2 · SAP BW/4HANA PCE — The Extended Runway

Overview

Convert or lift to BW/4HANA in Private Cloud Edition, gaining a supported path through 2040. You get HANA-optimized performance, simplified modelling, and initial exposure to BDC capabilities via the Data Product Generator.

Architecture

Option 2 · SAP BW/4HANA PCE  |  Maintenance to 2040

Convert BW objects to BW/4HANA in managed PCE. Simplified modeling and initial BDC exposure via Data Product Generator.

S/4HANA / ECC / Other sources → SAP BW/4HANA (HANA-native) → Data Product Generator (limited) → SAC / BO reporting

Limitation: Warehouse-centric ceiling remains. "Better old" rather than cloud-native new. Innovation gap widens over time.

 

The appeal

This feels like a real modernization move. The modelling paradigm is cleaner, HANA performance is materially better, and you're buying 15+ years of supported life. For organizations that have invested heavily in BW and want to preserve that investment while incrementally modernizing, this path feels responsible.

The reality check

The honest framing here is "better old" rather than truly new. BW/4HANA is still a warehouse-centric architecture at its core. You're not going to be building intelligent, composable data products or running embedded AI agents off a BW/4HANA foundation the way you can on a native BDC or lakehouse architecture. The 2040 maintenance date is reassuring—but the innovation gap may become uncomfortable well before then.

Best suited for: SAP-committed organizations with significant BW/4HANA conversion work already underway, or those for whom a greenfield re-platform is genuinely not feasible in the near term.

Option 3 · Greenfield BDC — Custom Data Products + Accelerators

Overview

A complete architectural reset. Zero BW. Sources (S/4HANA, ECC, and others) are extracted directly, modelled in SAP Datasphere, and delivered as custom and derived data products. AI agents and implementation accelerators automate significant portions of model builds, semantic layer enrichment, and data product generation.

Architecture

Option 3 · BDC Greenfield — Custom Data Products + Accelerators

Zero BW. Direct source extraction into Datasphere, modeled as custom/derived data products. AI agents and partner accelerators automate semantic enrichment and model builds.

S/4HANA · ECC · 3rd party → SAP Datasphere (semantic modeling) → Custom / derived data products → AI Data Studio agents → SAC · Intelligent apps · APIs

Accelerator advantage: Partner-built tooling compresses model build timelines significantly. Pre-built content reduces blank-page risk.

Investment: Highest upfront redesign effort. Business logic re-engineering required. Strong change management needed.

 

The appeal

This is the path generating the most excitement in architect conversations right now, and for good reason. It breaks the BW dependency entirely, aligns to the direction SAP is actually investing in, and opens the door to genuinely modern capabilities: composable data products, real AI integration, intelligent applications, and cloud-native scalability. Well-designed accelerator tooling has demonstrated material productivity gains—in some cases compressing what would be months of manual build work into weeks.

The reality check

This is also the highest-investment path upfront. Greenfield means greenfield—existing models don't migrate, business logic must be re-examined and re-implemented, and the organisational change management burden is real. The question isn't whether this path is technically superior (for most organizations, it is). The question is whether your organization has the capacity, sponsorship, and appetite for the transformation effort required.

Best suited for: Organizations ready to commit to a true platform shift, particularly those with S/4HANA or active ECC landscapes and a clear mandate to modernize analytics.

Option 4 · Greenfield BDC — SAP-Managed Data Products

Overview

Similar to Option 3, but leveraging SAP's own curated and managed data products as the foundation layer rather than fully custom-built data products. Integration with platforms like Databricks is supported. No BW dependency.

Architecture

Option 4 · BDC Greenfield — SAP-Managed Data Products

Zero BW. SAP-curated data products as foundation layer. Databricks integration for advanced analytics. Best suited for RISE with S/4HANA customers.

S/4HANA (RISE) + ECC (limited) → SAP Datasphere → SAP-managed data products (curated) → Databricks integration → SAC · Intelligent apps · APIs

Advantage: Lower blank-page risk. SAP-curated foundation reduces build effort for core business domains.

Constraint: Optimised for RISE with S/4HANA. ECC and hybrid landscapes face integration friction.

 

The appeal

SAP-managed data products represent a significant investment by SAP in pre-built, semantically enriched content covering core business domains. For organizations running RISE with S/4HANA, this path can significantly reduce the "blank page" problem—you're building on a curated foundation rather than starting from scratch.

The reality check

SAP's managed data products are currently best optimized for RISE with S/4HANA customers. Organizations running ECC, hybrid landscapes, or non-SAP source systems will encounter integration friction, access challenges, or additional build work that narrows the advantage.

Best suited for: RISE with S/4HANA customers looking for an SAP-native, lower-custom-development path to BDC adoption.

Option 5 · Re-platform to a Non-SAP Lakehouse or Data Platform

Overview

SAP source data—extracted via CDS views or other mechanisms, often with BDC handling the extraction and sharing layer—lands in a non-SAP platform of choice: Snowflake, Databricks, Google BigQuery, Microsoft Fabric, or Amazon Redshift. BW is eliminated entirely. Analytics and AI/ML are built natively on the target platform.

Architecture

SAP data extracted via CDS views and BDC APIs, landed directly into a non-SAP target platform. BW eliminated entirely. Analytics and AI/ML built natively on the target platform.

Extraction layer:
S/4HANA · ECC · SAP apps → CDS views / BDC Data Sharing APIs / ETL

Target platforms (choose one):
Snowflake Databricks Microsoft Fabric Google BigQuery Amazon Redshift

Consumption:
BI / analytics layer Native ML / AI models Data apps / APIs Non-SAP data unification

Important nuance: Even on this path, BDC typically handles clean SAP data extraction and sharing. Full SAP bypass is more complex than it appears.

Key advantages: Maximum flexibility · cost control · best-of-breed AI/ML · no SAP ecosystem lock-in · non-SAP data unification.

Key constraints: Highest rebuild effort · business logic re-engineering required · strong data engineering team essential.

 

The appeal

Maximum flexibility. You're no longer constrained by SAP's licensing model, release cadence, or ecosystem boundaries. AI and ML capabilities on platforms like Databricks and BigQuery are mature, deep, and actively evolving. Cost control is real. And for organizations with significant non-SAP data to unify with SAP data, this path eliminates integration awkwardness.

The reality check

This path demands the most migration work and the deepest rebuild. Business logic encoded in BW transformations doesn't port automatically—it requires deliberate re-engineering. Even on this path, BDC typically plays a role in clean extraction and sharing of SAP data, so the idea of completely bypassing the SAP data layer is more complex than it initially appears.

Best suited for: Organizations with strong data engineering capabilities, significant non-SAP data integration requirements, or a strategic commitment to platform independence and best-of-breed architecture.

The Bottom Line: Where the Momentum Is Building

Across conversations on the ground in 2026, a clear pattern is emerging. The PCE options are being chosen by organizations that need to buy time, not by organizations with genuine transformation ambition. They're legitimate decisions for the right circumstances, but few architecture leaders describe them as where they want to end up.

The real energy is in the greenfield re-platform paths—either to native BDC or to a non-SAP lakehouse. The driving force is AI. Organizations that can see what's possible when analytics and intelligence are natively integrated are struggling to get excited about warehouse-centric architectures, regardless of how long the maintenance window extends.

The practical hurdles are consistent across every conversation:

  • Rework effort — The sheer volume of business logic, calculation rules, and custom transformations encoded in mature BW environments is sobering.
  • Preserving deep business logic — Much of the logic in long-running BW systems isn't well-documented. Migration is as much a knowledge recovery exercise as a technical one.
  • Licensing and timeline — The commercial complexity of BDC licensing, RISE entitlements, and overlap with existing BW investments is a real architectural constraint.
  • Skills availability — Datasphere, BDC, and native lakehouse architectures require skill sets that are in high demand and not evenly distributed.

The Question Worth Sitting With

The migration off SAP BW isn't primarily a technology question—it's a strategic one. The technology options are well-defined. What varies by organization is the honest assessment of transformation capacity, the clarity of the analytics strategy, and the willingness to invest now to avoid a harder reckoning later.

Where is your organization leaning? SAP-native BDC greenfield, accelerated custom build, or full non-SAP platform independence? And what's your biggest real constraint—rework effort, preserving business logic, licensing complexity, or the skills gap?

The architects who navigate this best in the next 24 months won't be the ones who picked the objectively "right" platform. They'll be the ones who were clearest about what their organization could actually execute—and built a path that matched that reality.

SAP BW is a powerful enterprise data warehousing solution designed to consolidate, transform, and manage data from diverse sources. This data is then used for reporting, analysis, and informed decision-making.

SAP BW/4HANA represents a complete redesign, built exclusively on SAP HANA. This version prioritizes simplification and streamlining, reducing the complexity of data modeling and management. The number of data objects and layers is significantly reduced, making the system easier to understand and maintain.

So how can you upgrade your SAP BW knowledge to SAP BW/4HANA?

The SAP Certified - SAP BW/4HANA Delta certification (https://learning.sap.com/certifications/sap-certified-specialist-sap-bw-4hana-delta?searchId=f7594d89-3350-4740-ad14-e331c718a204&listPosition=2) verifies that you possess the knowledge of implementing and modeling SAP BW/4HANA required by the profile of an SAP BW/4HANA consultant.

entry.title: SAP BW Bridge or Data Product Generator (DPG): What would you choose
entry.content:
Ankit Sarkar 

  • Certified SAP Datasphere and Databricks Consultant
  • RG Technologies (2+ years of experience)

 

SAP BW Bridge and Data Product Generator (DPG)

Introduction

A common question arises - Should you expose your data for modern consumption, or should you migrate your BW system?

Organisations are moving from traditional on-premise BW systems to the cloud. So, the above question commonly arises.

The solution is BW Bridge and Data Product Generator (DPG). SAP offers two powerful options to migrate your BW system. You may see that they seem similar at first, but there are some huge differences between how they serve for your transformation journey.

SAP BW Bridge - Lift Your System to the Cloud: 

BW Bridge provides a way to migrate your existing BW system to the cloud with minimal disruption.

  • You can reuse the objects like DSOs, Info-Objects, and Transformations from the existing BW system.
  • You can entertain ABAP-based extraction logics.
  • You can keep on using classic extractors from SAP ECC and SAP S/4HANA.
  • Within SAP Datasphere, you can operate in a dedicated ABAP-enabled environment.

Use Cases : 

  • Companies use BW Bridge to move on-premise SAP/4HANA or SAP BW 7.x systems to SAP Datasphere without rebuilding data structures from scratch.
  • Organisations that excessively count on complex SAP S/API or ODP extractors, so with common methods, you can't connect directly to the cloud. Then you need the BW Bridge to connect with the cloud.
  • BW Bridge offers a staging area for complex transformations and cleaning before making the data available in Datasphere.

 SAP Data Product Generator (DPG) : 

You can use a different approach with DPG, instead of moving the whole system, DPG focuses on preparing your BW data usable in modern ecosystems like SAP Datasphere and Databricks.

  • You can replicate Info-Providers.
  • In tools like SAP Analytics Cloud or platforms like Databricks, you can do zero-copy consumption.
  • With the process chain, you can apply filters and schedule loads.
  • You can carry through full and delta data extraction.

Use Cases : 

  • When you need to migrate an on-premise BW system to a cloud system, you also need to keep the existing logics.
  • When you need to enable BW Info-providers in SAP Datasphere.
  • When you need to quickly bring out data models in Datasphere.
  • You need to perform AI/ML modelling with an external platform like Databricks, then you can share trusted, structured BW data with it.

 

Differences Between SAP BW Bridge and Data Product Generator (DPG) : 

AspectsSAP BW BridgeData Product Generator (DPG)
Core PurposeBW systems migrationReusable data products creation
Main FocusData Processing & Data WarehousingData Consumption & Data Sharing
Architecture RoleData Transformation and Data StorageData Reuse and Data Exposure
LayerModelling Layer or BackendBusiness Layer or Consumption
Data TransformationCan use data Transformation (ETL Logic)Cannot use Data Transformation
Data ModellingSupports full BW ModellingModelling is not used in DPG
Data Product CreationBW Bridge does not create any Data ProductData Product Creation is the core functionality of DPG
Data Storage It can store and manage dataIt uses the existing data
FlexibilityLess Flexible (BW Structure)More Flexible (Modern Approach)
ReusabilityLessHigh
Use CaseBW to Datasphere MigrationCurated Datasets sharing
Cloud Native To some extentCompletely 
Modern RelevanceLagacy MigrationFuture ready
Target UsersBW Developer or Data EngineersData Consumers or Business Users

Conclusion 

If you are shifting to SAP Datasphere, this is a common confusion about which service you need to use. 

In this Blog, I have explained some differences, use cases, and some practical examples or ways so you can decide which service you would use, whether you want to migrate your BW system or explore your data for a modern approach.

entry.title: How to Prepare for Your System-Based SAP BW/4HANA Certification
entry.content:
SAP BW, especially in its SAP-HANA-optimized version, SAP BW∕4HANA, is still the most widely used data warehousing solution with SAP. Consultants for SAP BW/4HANA are continuously highly requested by many enterprises. Whether you want to help within such SAP BW/4HANA projects, want to demonstrate your knowledge within your own organization, or apply for a new position – by proving your skills in this area, you can increase your chances.

 

So how do you prove your expertise? 

Understanding the certification format

You may have read or heard that SAP has re-designed the “SAP Certified - Data Engineer - SAP BW/4HANA” and the “SAP Certified - SAP BW/4HANA Delta“ certification. You now need to perform system-based tasks in a real system to verify that you possess the core skills required in the role of a Data Engineer in the SAP BW/4HANA area. It’s not just about memorizing concepts but actually applying them in a system. Check out this page with FAQ and an onboarding video that explains it:

https://learning.sap.com/certifications/sap-certified-associate-reporting-modelling-and-data-acquisition-with-sap-bw-4hana/exam?onboarding=true

You won’t be asked to simply define terms, but you’ll need to do the work, within a time limit of 180 minutes. This means, your preparation must be heavily practice oriented. Unlike theoretical exams, our hands-on certifications test your ability to navigate the SAP environment, build data models, and demonstrate real-world competency.

You should especially be able to demonstrate the following skills:

  • Creating sources and provisioning data from them,
  • Creating physical and virtual SAP BW/4HANA models,
  • Creating a data flow and filling data targets,
  • Applying concepts like data transformation, including data lookup, unit conversion, and currency translation,
  • Creating queries in SAP BW/4HANA,
  • Implementing authorizations in SAP BW/4HANA.

On the other hand, like in a real project situation, it’s now an open book exam: You are allowed to use any material or online resource to guide you, for example to find a transaction code or table name.

But don’t rely on looking up concepts or practical procedures: There is not much time to complete the certification tasks.

 

How Should You Prepare?

1. Review the theory:

Before diving into system-based preparation, it’s essential to understand what you’re preparing for.

Even though the exam is practical, you still need to understand the underlying concepts. Make sure you’re comfortable with:

  • Standard SAP BW architecture and exceptional options,
  • Data modeling layers (Staging, Harmonization, Reporting),
  • The purpose of specific objects and object types (e.g., InfoObjects vs ADSOs vs CompositeProviders),
  • Data flow processes (Extraction → Transformation → Loading)

 

2. Perform the course exercises:

Even though the exam tasks are different from the course exercises (which means, copying existing solution objects will not work for you), they are inspired by them. Therefore, invest most of your preparation time into repeating the exercises of our instructor-led trainings BW405, BW410, BW430, BW450, and BW465 – or demonstrations within the corresponding online material. Check the following blog for a list of the required courses:

https://community.sap.com/t5/data-and-analytics-learning-group-blog-posts/how-to-learn-sap-bw-4hana-and-get-certified/ba-p/14307472

 

Make sure that you know where you find the settings needed to fulfil the requirements of these exercises.

 

If you want to practice outside the setting of a classroom training, book an SAP Practice System similar to the ones that are used in the instructor-led class. Click here:

https://learning.sap.com/practice-systems?page=1

 

3. Practice your own example scenarios:

Some task steps of the system-based certification depend on earlier steps of the same certification. Therefore, try to think about a larger scenario. For example:

  • Create a DataSource in a source system
  • Replicate it to SAP BW.
  • Load data from the source.
  • Transform it.
  • Store it in an ADSO.

 

4. Timing and Quality management:

Hands-on exams are time-bound. It’s not enough to know how to do something—you must do it efficiently.

  • Practice tasks with a timer.
  • Identify steps where you slow down and intensify your training here.
  • Learn shortcuts and navigation tricks. For example, try to start a new exercise while a loading mechanism takes time without forgetting to return to the result for final steps.
  • Simulate exam conditions as much as possible.
  • Let someone else give you tasks and try to fulfil them as good as you can, even if something might be unclear to you.

In the system-based assessment, you will not be notified if you made an error. At the end, you submit the entire work, and then, there is no chance to correct it. So, focus on ways to test yourself if the objects you created really work as desired.

The technical object names are a crucial part of our verification mechanism. Train to be careful when creating the object names with the correct name. Pay attention to “_” (underscore).

Create a checklist of your common errors and review it before the exam.

 

5. Live Sessions

In addition to courses and practice systems, the SAP Learning portal offers live sessions that are useful for learning guidelines. Use especially the “Get Certified with BW/4HANA” series, starting on May 5th to ask questions. Click here to book it:

https://learning.sap.com/live-sessions/get-certified-sap-certified-data-engineer-sap-bw-4hana  

These sessions are delivered by subject-matter-experts (SMEs) from SAP Training

Just click below to explore our live sessions:

https://learning.sap.com/live-sessions 

 

 

Taking the Certification Exam

When you feel prepared enough, it's time to take the certification exam.

Just click below for information and booking the certifications:

https://learning.sap.com/certifications/sap-certified-specialist-sap-bw-4hana-delta

https://learning.sap.com/certifications/sap-certified-associate-reporting-modelling-and-data-acquisition-with-sap-bw-4hana

Book a time (see the image) when you will not be disturbed. 

 

Make sure that you take the exam in a place where you won’t be interrupted and with good internet. (If the internet connection is lost, you can log in again without losing your objects, but you’ll lose time.)

Make sure that you use the correct version of the tools as indicated in the task description.

As stated avove, make sure that you create objects exactly in the way it is demanded - especially regarding the technical names.

If something goes wrong:

  • Don’t panic
  • Check previous steps systematically
  • Fix the issue and move on

Remember: the exam is testing your practical problem-solving ability—not perfection 70% is enough.

Make sure that you really submit your work before the time is up.

entry.title: Building a Sales Order Backlog Report Using Custom CDS Views (Sales + Billing)
entry.content:
Amartya Ghosh Dastidar, Senior SAP Developer


Introduction

Core Data Services (CDS) views are central to data modelling in SAP S/4HANA. A frequent requirement in the Sales and Distribution (SD) area is a sales order backlog report — the value and quantity of customer orders that have been placed but not yet invoiced. This post explains how to build such a report using custom CDS views that combine the Sales and Billing domains, covering the key techniques involved: joins, aggregation, calculated fields, type casting, null handling, and the correct treatment of cancelled and pro-forma invoices.

Prerequisites

  • SAP S/4HANA system with ABAP Development Tools (ADT) in Eclipse
  • Basic knowledge of ABAP CDS and SQL
  • Familiarity with SD documents (sales orders, billing documents) and the display transactions VA03 / VF03

Understanding the Sales Order Backlog

In SD, a customer order flows through a chain of documents before revenue is recognised:

Sales Order  --->  Outbound Delivery  --->  Billing Document

            (delivery backlog)        (billing backlog)

The term “backlog” can refer to either of two gaps in this chain:

  1. Delivery backlog — orders placed but not yet delivered.
  2. Billing backlog — orders placed but not yet invoiced.

The report described here implements the billing view, defined as Backlog = Ordered Value − Billed Value. This definition determines the data model, because it requires the Sales domain and the Billing domain to be combined rather than reading open order quantities alone.

Standard CDS Views Used

The report is built on top of two released standard CDS views:

  1. I_SalesOrderItem — sales order line items (ordered quantity and net value).
  2. I_BillingDocumentItem — billing document line items (invoiced quantity and net value), which reference the originating sales order line via SalesDocument and SalesDocumentItem.

Solution Architecture

The solution uses a two-view (layered) design:

  1. ZIC_LIVEBILLING (helper view) — returns only valid, non-cancelled invoices per sales order item.
  2. ZIC_SALES_BACKLOG (main view) — joins the sales order item to the helper, aggregates billing, and calculates the backlog.

The layering is necessary because the cancellation logic requires a self-join that cannot be expressed inline within an aggregating view on all CDS compiler releases. Isolating it in a helper view also keeps the cleaning logic in one place and results in a cleaner, more maintainable model.

Step 1: Create the Helper View (ZIC_LIVEBILLING)

This view filters the billing document items down to genuine, live invoices — excluding pro-forma documents, cancellation documents, and cancelled originals.

Explanation

  1. SDDocumentCategory = 'M' — keeps only invoice-type documents; excludes pro-forma invoices.
  2. CancelledBillingDocument = '' — excludes the cancellation documents themselves.
  3. The self-join on C.CancelledBillingDocument = B.BillingDocument links each invoice to any document that cancelled it. The condition C.BillingDocument is null then keeps only invoices that were never cancelled, removing the cancelled originals.

Step 2: Create the Main View (ZIC_SALES_BACKLOG)

The main view joins the sales order item to the cleaned billing data, aggregates the billed values, and derives the backlog.

Key Techniques Explained

  1. Aggregation with GROUP BY — a single order line can be billed across several invoices (partial billing). Summing the billing per order key collapses these into one row and prevents the ordered value from being multiplied.
  2. Type casting — currency amounts of different internal lengths cannot be subtracted directly. Casting all amounts to abap.curr(23,2) (and quantities to abap.quan(13,3)) ensures type compatibility.
  3. COALESCE for null handling — an order line with no invoice returns null from the join; coalesce(..., 0) converts null to zero so the arithmetic remains valid.
  4. Calculated fields — the backlog quantity and value are derived inline as ordered minus billed.
  5. Session date — dats_days_between(RequestedDeliveryDate, $session.system_date) produces the number of days a line is overdue, enabling aging analysis.

Business Logic: Counting Only Valid Billing

Accurate backlog depends on summing only genuine, live invoices. Three categories must be excluded:

  1. Pro-forma invoices — not real sales; excluded via SDDocumentCategory = 'M'.
  2. Cancelled invoices — a cancelled invoice and its cancellation document both remain in the table; the self-join in the helper view removes both, leaving only the live invoice.
  3. Rejected order items — lines with a rejection reason are excluded via SalesDocumentRjcnReason = ''.

Note: the field that stores the cancellation reference can vary by release and may sit on the cancellation document rather than the original. The self-join approach is robust to this, because it identifies cancelled documents from the relationship rather than from a single status field.

Validation

The view should be validated against the source documents (VA03, VF03, and document flow) across the main data patterns:

  • Never billed — no invoice in the flow; backlog equals the full order value.
  • Partially billed — invoice covers part of the order; backlog equals the remaining value and quantity.
  • Fully billed — invoice equals the order; backlog is zero.
  • Cancelled invoice — only the live invoice is counted; backlog reflects the remaining value.

Where source data itself is inconsistent (for example a negatively priced item or a mis-keyed invoice amount), the view reflects the source faithfully. A reporting view should not silently correct source data; such cases are data-quality issues to be flagged separately.

Standard vs Custom CDS Views

Standard delivery/open-order backlog content is appropriate where a vanilla delivery backlog with standard fields is required. A custom view is justified when the requirement differs, as in this case:

  • The metric is ordered − billed (a billing backlog), which standard content does not frame the same way.
  • It combines Sales and Billing into one pre-shaped row with the specific fields and aging logic required for reporting.
  • It encodes system-specific billing rules (pro-forma and cancellation handling) validated against actual documents.

The trade-off is ongoing maintenance. Where standard content satisfies the same definition, it should be preferred to reduce maintenance overhead.

Key Points to Remember

  • Clarify the backlog definition (delivery vs billing) before designing the view.
  • The SQL view name is limited to 16 characters.
  • Aggregate one-to-many relationships before joining to avoid duplication.
  • Cast all amounts and quantities to a common type before arithmetic.
  • Exclude pro-forma, cancelled, and rejected documents from billed totals.
  • Use a layered design when complex filtering cannot be expressed inline.
  • Validate the output against source documents before release.
