entry.title: Trade wide composite keys for a narrow hash surrogate key
entry.content:
In this post I want to share a small pattern that helped me speed up some SQLScript and AMDP code in HANA (BW/4HANA scenario): swapping a wide composite key for one small hash key instead. I'll go through why it works, show a short code example, and share what happened when I tried it on a real production routine, along with a couple of things worth watching out for before you use it yourself.

If you write SQLScript or AMDP code in HANA, you may group, join, or partition data on ten or more columns at once. When the key gets this wide, performance often gets worse. This happens in many places: master data lookups with a long key, dimension joins that carry many columns just to match, or running balances and YTD calculations that use many fields as the key.
The fix is always the same. Do not carry the wide key through every step. Instead, build one small hash key early, and use only this key in the steps between. Add the wide columns back one time, at the end.

The reason this helps is that in HANA, a hash join or partition gets more expensive the wider the key is, not just when you have more rows. So with a fifteen-column key, every step that touches it pays for that width again, even though most of those columns aren't actually needed until you write the final result.
-- build the narrow key once, early
lt_keyed = SELECT c.*,
                  HASH_MD5( key_col1 || '|' || key_col2 || '|' || key_col3
                            || '|' || key_col4 || '|' || key_col5 ) AS dim_key
           FROM :lt_clean AS c;

-- the dimension - one row per key, added back only at the end
lt_dim   = SELECT DISTINCT dim_key, key_col1, key_col2, key_col3, key_col4, key_col5
           FROM :lt_keyed;

-- everything in between (grouping, joins, window functions) uses dim_key only

-- add the wide columns back, one time, at the end
outtab   = SELECT d.key_col1, d.key_col2, d.key_col3, d.key_col4, d.key_col5, b.result
           FROM :lt_result AS b
           INNER JOIN :lt_dim AS d ON b.dim_key = d.dim_key;
The wide columns now travel through the routine only two times, once at the start and once at the end. This is where most of the benefit comes from.
One real example: I used this method in a production running-balance routine, with a key based on a few financial fields (ledger, company code, account, fiscal year). Together with a small DTP fix and removing a duplicate-record issue, the load time went from about 53 minutes to 37 minutes, and the number of output rows dropped by almost half. I cannot say the hash key alone caused all of this, since we changed a few things at once, but it made every group-by and window step much lighter to run. The same idea works well for a wide master data join too, or any place where your key becomes too large.
Worth keeping in mind before you use this everywhere: computing the hash costs CPU time on every row, and building the small key table isn't free either, so on a small package HANA might already handle the wide key just fine and you'd just be adding work for nothing, so measure first. And don't save this hash as a real business key anywhere, it's meant to live inside one routine, not become something other objects start depending on.

So to sum up, this post covered a way to deal with wide join and group-by keys in HANA: hash the wide columns into one narrow key early on, use that key everywhere in between, and only bring the real columns back at the very end. The main thing to take away is that this can meaningfully reduce workload of your grouping, joins, and partitioning once your key grows past a few columns, but it's not free, so it's worth measuring on your own data rather than applying it everywhere by default.
Has anyone seen this go the other way, where the hash made things slower? What was the package size in that case?

entry.title: Feeding HANA input parameters from a BW query prompt, without the user noticing
entry.content:
This post is about a pattern I use to push a BW query's filter values down into a HANA Calculation View, so the view can restrict its data early instead of scanning everything first. I'll walk through the two variables you need, how a reference InfoObject makes them work together, and a simple code skeleton for the exit that connects them.

The problem: filtering too late

If a Calculation View sits behind a BW query and has no input parameter driving it, it usually has to build or scan its full working set before BW ever gets a chance to filter anything. Years of history, every version, everything. Only after that does the BW-level filter cut it down. For a view with a lot of periods or a lot of versions behind it, that is a lot of wasted work before any actual filtering happens.

Not fun to debug either, from the outside it just looks like "the query is slow," and you end up in the Calculation View long before you think to check whether an input parameter is even being used.

 

The fix is to let the Calculation View filter itself early, using an input parameter fed directly from what the user selects in the query. The part that takes a bit of thought is that the value going into that input parameter usually needs some derivation logic behind it, and you don't want to build that logic into a variable the user has to fill in themselves.

Two variables, one job each

That is where a reference InfoObject comes in. You create a technical copy of your real characteristic that just points back to the original one, and you use that reference object in your query instead of the original. On it, you put two variables. The first is a normal, mandatory, user-facing variable, the one that shows up on the selection screen and the one people actually fill in. The second is a customer exit variable, set to run after the prompt (i_step = 2). It is not flagged as ready for input, so it never appears on the selection screen in the first place, there's no prompt to hide because it was never going to ask anything.

 

Why a second InfoObject, and not just a second variable

You might wonder why you need a second InfoObject at all, instead of just putting both variables on the original characteristic. Took me a confused afternoon to figure this part out. The reason sits in the CompositeProvider mapping itself. The Calculation View's underlying field shows up there twice: once as a normal field, carrying the view's actual value up into BW for reporting, and once again under a separate "input parameters" node, which is where you feed a value back down into the view to filter it. Those are two different directions of communication, on two different mapping slots, and the original characteristic is already busy handling the first one. You need a second field to hang the second direction on, and that is what the reference InfoObject gives you, without duplicating any master data or touching how the original field already works.

 

The exit itself

The exit variable's ABAP code reads whatever the user entered in the first variable (or in a couple of other prompted variables, if you need to combine values), does whatever logic you need on it, and returns the result as a single value. That result is what actually gets mapped to the Calculation View's input parameter, in the CompositeProvider or transformation where you connect BW variables to HANA parameters. The user only ever sees and fills in the first variable, the second one just does its work quietly in the background.

A simplified version of the exit logic looks like this:

WHEN 'ZZ_MY_EXIT_VARIABLE'.

  IF i_step = 2.

    READ TABLE i_t_var_range INTO l_s_var_range
      WITH KEY vnam = 'ZZ_USER_INPUT_VARIABLE'.

    IF sy-subrc = 0 AND l_s_var_range-low IS NOT INITIAL.

      " do whatever transformation or combination logic you need here
      l_derived_value = l_s_var_range-low.

      CLEAR l_s_range.
      l_s_range-sign = 'I'.
      l_s_range-opt  = 'EQ'.
      l_s_range-low  = l_derived_value.
      APPEND l_s_range TO e_t_range.

    ENDIF.

  ENDIF.

Getting the i_step handling right took a couple of tries, the documentation on customer exits assumes you already half know what you're doing. The logic inside can be as simple as passing the value straight through, or as involved as combining two or three prompted variables, applying a fallback when something is blank, or clamping the result to a safe range so the view never accidentally opens up years of data by mistake. All of that stays hidden inside the exit. The user experience does not change at all, they still just see one field to fill in.

Did it actually help

I pulled runtime stats for one of the queries running this pattern, before and after the filters/input parameters were in place.

So that's the setup: a reference InfoObject, one variable the user fills in, one exit variable doing the derivation, mapped into the view's input parameter. None of it is exotic once you've seen it once, it just took a wrong turn or two to get there.

One thing worth watching for if you build something similar: compare full year-plus-period values, not just the bare period number, when deciding which of two source variables wins. We didn't, at first, and it worked fine right up until one of the two source variables happened to resolve to a different year than the other. Bare-period comparison doesn't know that, and it took a strange data window to notice.

Wrapping up

To wrap up, this post covered how to feed a BW query's user input into a HANA Calculation View's input parameter without adding a second visible prompt variable: a reference InfoObject carrying one user-facing variable and one customer exit variable that does the actual derivation, mapped into the view's input parameter through the CompositeProvider. If a Calculation View behind your query is scanning more than it needs to, this pattern is worth trying, and on the query I measured it against it cut runtime by close to 5.5x.

entry.title: Another Way of solving the 2bn SID Limit of BW[4] InfoObject Characteristics
entry.content:
Dear BW enthusiasts!

As we all know, SIDs  are central elements behind InfoObject Characteristics  in SAP BW or BW/4HANA, and core functions like InfoCube designs, navigational attributes, and query processing rely on them.

And we all should know, there can only be 2 billion different values for one single InfoObject Characteristic: This is a hard limit based on the technical INT4 representation in the ABAP DDIC. To be clear: The limit is exactly 2.000.000.000 (!), as additional values are reserved for internal BW use - changing the maximum is not allowed/possible by any means.

In reality, it is not a rare case that values keep growing over years in customer systems and, for whatever reason, they get close to the mentioned 2bn limit. Hitting the limit results in immediate failure of data loads with short dumps of type UNCAUGHT_EXCEPTION in CL_RSR_RRSI_SERVICE=>GET_NUMBER… FORM SAPLRRSI … SIDS_CREATE… . All of the sudden, no data can be loaded any more!

Due to this critical effect, your system should trigger alerts (e.g. via the SAP SolMan Early Watch Alert Reports section “Number Range Buffering for BW Objects” e.g.) starting from a threshold of 1.5bn to provide customers reaction time. The central note for this topic is 1331403 and it states the urgency very clearly:
When you have crossed the 1 billion mark, it is time to think about the future slowly.
If you crossed 1.5 billion, you should think about that soon.
Crossing 1.9 billion calls for immediate attention.

While notes 1331403 and 2530410 provide detailed (but complex) guidance on how to analyze and solve the situation, there is a lean solution alternative if your system runs on SAP HANA: Untie the InfoObject and get rid of SIDs completely!
In terms of configuration this means switching on the “High Cardinality” property in the InfoObject data model. This feature is available since years in both BW 7.5 and BW/4HANA – but it is often overlooked during application design (or was not available when the InfoObject was created). Such change in live applications is normally tricky, but this one can be done by the BW remodeling toolbox with little effort as only meta data has to be changed and the existing SID-table is dropped.
 

Preconditions of leveraging the "High Cardinality" property

As the “High Cardinality” property wipes out SIDs completely, BW functions relying on them are then not supported any more. So carefully validate following conditions before considering this approach:
The facts are, that “High-Cardinality” InfoObject Characteristics...

  • cannot be used as a navigation attribute,
  • cannot be used in hierarchies,
  • cannot be the parent in a compounding relationship to another Characteristic,
  • cannot be used in InfoCubes; they can only be used in InfoProviders like ADSOs that store the semantic value rather than the SIDs of the included InfoObjects,
  • limit the ADSO master data check to “no master data check/no reporting” or “master data check during reporting”, and
  • cannot be used in APDs (meaning the famous SAP HANA Analysis Processes, only available in BW 7.5)

Reporting on "High-Cardinality" InfoObjects is not impacted. But, as OLAP engine relies on SIDs, those are generated on the fly as temporary local SIDs during processing. The resulting performance penalty is compensated by the fact, that "High-Cardinality" InfoObjects are HASH partitioned at the first level as opposed to normal Characteristics. That helps particularly in terms of how the data is stored and accessed, leading to better performance for read and write operations (see SAP note 3404208).

Side note: This property is only available for Characteristics of data types CHAR or NUMC with a length >= 10, because a length <10 will never reach the 2 bn limit.

Validation & Adjustment via the BW Remodeling toolbox

After you checked that the restrictions are not a showstopper in your scenario, set up a remodeling rule in Tr. RSMRT and use the Simulate function for the real test: It will provide a positive or negative answer based on the preconditions mentioned above. See also 3487041 (Activate High Cardinality for InfoObject via Remodeling Toolbox) for a step-by-step guidance. 

In case the simulation is ok, you can execute the remodeling rule and transport it to the next tier afterward. In the negative case, try to identify the restriction(s) and evaluate possibilities to remove them. For instance, the InfoObject is navigation attribute in another Characteristic... but if that navigation object is not used in any BW Query, then it should be fine changing it to display attribute only.

"Decision Tree"
(1) Validate the data growth first: If your estimation results in hitting the limit in year 2237 only, no action is required (best case).
(2) If many unique new records are created regularly and 2bn values are reached in near future - check if changing to "High-Cardinality" is possible and try leveraging this concept (good case).
(3) If both validations are negative, go on as described in SAP notes 1331403 and 2530410: Find out if there are gaps in the SID number range you could use (ok cases, referred to as C_1, C_2_C3). If that is also negative, then (4) full redesign is the only option (worst case, C_ALL).

Summary
The purpose of this blog post is to outline another approach to solve SID challenges in high-volume data scenarios. Deleting master data values, adjusting the SID number range, replacing troublesome InfoObjects in existing data flows or a application redesign can be tiring and mostly ends in considerable efforts. In some situations, remodeling your master data to “High-Cardinality” might be a really good and lean approach to get ahead.

Key Sources
1331403 - SIDs, Numberranges and BW Infoobjects
2530410 - How To proceed in case the number range limit of an InfoObject is reached
3404208 - How to check the high cardinality flag for an InfoObject Characteristic
3487041 - Activate High Cardinality for InfoObject via Remodeling Toolbox (RSMRT)
SAP BW/4HANA help > Modeling InfoObject Characteristics
SAP Support help > Master Data Tables
SAP Support help > Data Modeling Overview

Thanks Vadim and Tom for sharing your experiences.

entry.title: SAP BW Diet Strategy: How to Reduce Your SAP BW Footprint on the Path to SAP Business Data Cloud
entry.content:
Introduction

Moving an existing SAP BW landscape to the cloud is not only a technical migration exercise. It is also an opportunity to review the current BW footprint, reduce unnecessary HANA memory consumption, optimize TCO, and decide which workloads should remain in BW and which ones can benefit from SAP Business Data Cloud capabilities.

SAP Business Data Cloud opens new possibilities for existing SAP BW customers: BW data can be exposed to modern data fabric scenarios, combined with new data in SAP Datasphere, used in AI and ML scenarios, and gradually modernized without requiring everything to be transformed at once. At the same time, cloud infrastructure cost can make the existing BW footprint an important factor in the target architecture.

This leads to a simple question:

How can we put an SAP BW system on a “diet” before or during the move to SAP Business Data Cloud?

The answer is not a single migration pattern. Different InfoProviders and data flows may require different strategies.

A flexible strategy, not a single migration path

The framework below summarizes the alternatives I use when discussing a BW diet strategy with customers and partners.

Figure 1 – SAP Business Data Cloud – BW Diet Strategy overview

The overview starts with Housekeeping as step zero and then presents five possible paths: Lift & Shift, Convert & Lift, Lift & Optimize, Lift & Split, and Lift & Transform. Each one has a different balance between effort, memory reduction, modernization, front-end impact, and adoption of new SAP BDC capabilities.

One important principle is that these approaches do not necessarily need to be applied to the entire BW system. In many landscapes, the best results will come from evaluating InfoProviders and data flows individually, or grouping them according to similar characteristics and requirements.

0. Housekeeping: the mandatory starting point

Before discussing cloud architecture, data tiering, or the new modeling capabilities available in SAP Datasphere, the first question should be much simpler:

Do we still need all the data and objects currently occupying the BW system?

Unused InfoProviders, obsolete queries, historical staging layers, old flows, and redundant persistencies should be carefully reviewed before being carried over to the new cloud infrastructure.

The SAP BDC Free Assessment can be used as initial guidance to identify relevant objects and support the evaluation of each InfoProvider according to its actual usage and future purpose. Key questions include whether the provider has been used recently, whether data is still being loaded, whether planning is enabled, whether the data will still be required in the future — to be determined by the customer, using the assessment results as a starting point — and whether it may be relevant for future SAP BDC use cases.

This is important because housekeeping is normally the lowest-cost optimization opportunity.

Data that no longer requires high-performance access should be evaluated for a more appropriate and cost-efficient storage option rather than simply remaining in expensive in-memory storage.

The assessment can also help reveal a Pareto effect: in many BW systems, a relatively small number of objects accounts for a large percentage of total memory consumption. These objects should receive special attention during the BW Diet analysis.

1. Lift & Shift: preserve the existing BW landscape

The simplest approach is to move the existing SAP BW landscape to SAP Business Warehouse, private cloud edition in SAP Business Data Cloud, prioritizing continuity and minimizing redesign during the transition.

The main advantage is speed. Existing data models, InfoProviders, queries, source-system integrations, and front-end applications can remain largely unchanged, while BW data becomes available for integration with SAP Datasphere, SAP Analytics Cloud, SAP BDC Connect, SAP Databricks, SAP Snowflake and other SAP BDC capabilities.

This approach is particularly attractive when the main priorities are:

  • Fast cloud adoption
  • Low impact on users
  • Preservation of existing BW investments
  • Immediate availability of BW data for new SAP BDC use cases

However, there is an important limitation:

Lift & Shift alone is not a BW Diet strategy.

Housekeeping remains essential, since a pure Lift & Shift does not reduce the existing BW footprint or sizing by itself and may therefore result in higher Capacity Unit consumption.

In other words: Moving an oversized BW system to the cloud still gives you an oversized BW system — only in the cloud.

This is why, in a BW Diet scenario, Lift & Shift should follow the housekeeping phase. Before moving the system to the cloud, the existing footprint should first be reviewed and reduced wherever possible, so that only relevant data, models, and workloads are carried forward.

2. Convert & Lift: modernize BW itself

For SAP BW 7.x customers, another alternative is to convert to SAP BW/4HANA as part of the modernization journey.

The main advantage of this approach is the opportunity to simplify the existing BW data architecture while moving toward a more modern modeling framework based on LSA++ principles. SAP BW/4HANA reduces the number of modeling object types and provides greater control over data persistence and additional virtualization opportunities.

A conversion project can therefore be used to:

  • Simplify existing data models
  • Eliminate redundant persistence layers
  • Replace or modernize legacy BW objects
  • Increase the use of virtualization where appropriate
  • Establish a leaner data architecture before or during the move to SAP Business Data Cloud

This approach is particularly relevant when the objective is not only to move BW to the cloud, but also to use the transition as an opportunity to reduce technical debt and simplify the existing landscape.

SAP BW/4HANA also provides an important capability for data footprint optimization: Data Tiering Optimization (DTO), which can be combined with technologies such as Native Storage Extension (NSE) to reduce the amount of data that needs to remain in hot in-memory storage.

Compared with a Lift & Shift approach, Convert & Lift requires more transformation effort and a deeper assessment of the existing BW models. However, it can also result in a significantly leaner and more modern BW environment, providing a stronger foundation for further optimization and integration with SAP Business Data Cloud.

For customers with large historical data volumes, this modernization also opens the door to a more granular multi-temperature storage strategy, which leads to the next approach: Lift & Optimize.

3. Lift & Optimize: use multi-temperature storage

Not every byte in an SAP BW system requires the same level of performance.

Recent financial data queried every few minutes and ten-year-old historical data accessed only occasionally should not necessarily consume the same storage resources.

This is the idea behind a multi-temperature architecture:

Hot data remains in HANA in-memory storage to provide the highest performance.

Warm data can use technologies such as Native Storage Extension (NSE), where data remains managed by SAP HANA but does not need to reside entirely in memory.

Cold data can be placed in lower-cost storage technologies such as SAP IQ or SAP HANA Cloud, data lake Relational Engine, depending on the BW version and the target architecture.

The trade-off is straightforward: moving less frequently accessed data out of in-memory storage can significantly improve storage cost efficiency, while potentially resulting in slower access to warm or cold data.

SAP BW 7.5 on HANA: For SAP BW 7.5, Near-Line Storage can be used to reduce the amount of historical data stored directly in BW while keeping this information available for BW queries.

In addition, SAP Note 3715415 provides an NSE-based option for selected BW objects. With this approach, complete aDSOs, classic DSOs, or InfoCubes can be moved to page-loadable storage.

An important distinction is that this approach is not equivalent to Data Tiering Optimization in SAP BW/4HANA. The SAP BW 7.5 NSE option operates at the level of complete supported InfoProviders, whereas DTO provides a more granular and integrated data-tiering framework.

For this reason, the BW 7.5 NSE option should primarily be considered a capacity optimization mechanism, whereas DTO in SAP BW/4HANA provides more granular control over data tiering.

SAP BW/4HANA: With SAP BW/4HANA, Data Tiering Optimization provides greater flexibility to classify data according to its temperature and access patterns. Frequently accessed data can remain in-memory, while less frequently accessed data can be moved to warm or cold storage according to the selected architecture.

Lift & Optimize is particularly relevant when a significant portion of the BW footprint consists of historical or infrequently accessed data that must remain available, while preserving the existing BW consumption layer and avoiding a major redesign of the analytical landscape.

4. Lift & Split: keep BW, offload selected data to the SAP Datasphere Object Store

A more transformative option is to reduce the BW footprint by moving selected historical or low-usage data to the SAP Datasphere Object Store, while keeping frequently accessed and operational data in BW.

In a Lift & Split scenario, SAP BW continues to support the workloads that benefit from remaining in the existing environment, while SAP Datasphere becomes the consumption layer for the data that has been offloaded. This can be particularly useful for InfoProviders with large historical volumes or relatively low usage, where keeping all data in the BW in-memory environment may no longer be the most cost-efficient option.

Historical data can be moved to SAP Datasphere and stored in the Object Store, providing a more cost-optimized storage option while still making the data available for analytical and integration scenarios. Depending on the use case, frequently accessed data can remain in BW, while less frequently accessed information is managed in SAP Datasphere.

For some scenarios, recent data can remain in BW and be federated into SAP Datasphere, where it can be combined with historical data already stored in the cloud. Federation, however, should be carefully evaluated for high-volume scenarios due to the potential performance impact.

This approach is particularly relevant when the BW landscape contains a significant amount of historical data, some InfoProviders have relatively low usage, and there is enough flexibility to rebuild or redirect the analytical consumption layer.

The main trade-off is the additional implementation effort required to establish the new integration, analytical, and consumption layers in SAP Datasphere. Additionally, scenarios that combine federated BW data with data stored in SAP Datasphere should be carefully tested from a performance perspective.

5. Lift & Transform: redesign selected high-impact flows

The most transformative strategy does not require redesigning the entire BW landscape.

Instead, the focus is on identifying the data flows and InfoProviders that contribute most significantly to the overall BW memory footprint and selectively rebuilding those scenarios in SAP Datasphere, using capabilities such as the Object Store.

When a relatively small number of high-volume InfoProviders accounts for a significant percentage of total memory consumption, redesigning those flows can generate a meaningful footprint reduction while allowing the remaining BW landscape to follow a simpler migration path.

This is the essence of the Lift & Transform approach: transform where the impact is highest, while preserving the rest of the landscape where a redesign would not deliver sufficient storage optimization benefits to justify the additional effort.

The selected flows can be rebuilt natively in SAP Datasphere, leveraging modern modeling capabilities and, where appropriate, cost-optimized storage options. BW Model Transfer or semantic onboarding can also be considered as accelerators for selected scenarios.

This approach typically requires more implementation effort than data tiering or a pure Lift & Shift, but it can also provide greater architectural modernization, reduce technical debt, and create a stronger foundation for future SAP BDC use cases.

Lift & Transform is particularly relevant when a limited number of InfoProviders or data flows accounts for a disproportionately large share of HANA memory consumption and when there is enough flexibility to redesign the corresponding analytical scenarios.

There is no single BW Diet

The most important conclusion is that these strategies are not mutually exclusive. In most SAP BW landscapes, a combination of approaches will provide better results than applying a single migration strategy to the entire system.

Different parts of the landscape may require different decisions. Unused or obsolete content can be addressed through housekeeping, stable core BW models may follow a Lift & Shift approach, classic SAP BW 7.x scenarios may benefit from Convert & Lift, large historical providers may be candidates for Lift & Optimize, low-usage historical data can potentially be offloaded through Lift & Split, and selected high-memory data flows may justify a Lift & Transform approach.

The appropriate strategy should therefore be determined according to the characteristics, usage, business relevance, and technical requirements of each InfoProvider or data flow, either individually or in groups.

This is why the assessment phase is so important.

The first step is to understand where the BW footprint is concentrated, which objects are still actively used, how frequently the data is accessed, and which workloads will remain relevant in the target SAP BDC architecture. From there, the most significant InfoProviders can be identified and evaluated according to their business value, access patterns, technical complexity, and optimization potential.

The SAP BDC Assessment can provide a useful starting point by offering insights into the existing landscape, object usage, and potential optimization opportunities. This information can be complemented with SAP BW tools such as ST14 or DB02 to identify high-volume InfoProviders and understand where memory optimization efforts can generate the greatest impact.

The objective is not simply to reduce the BW footprint at any cost, but to determine the most appropriate treatment for each workload — whether that means housekeeping, data tiering, offloading, conversion, or redesign.

Ultimately, a successful BW Diet Strategy is about focusing transformation efforts where they provide meaningful technical and economic benefits, while preserving existing investments where modernization would add limited value.

 Final thoughts

Moving SAP BW to SAP Business Data Cloud should not be viewed only as an infrastructure migration.

It is also an opportunity to ask a more fundamental question: Which parts of the existing BW landscape still require high-performance in-memory resources, and which parts could be optimized through housekeeping, data tiering, offloading, or redesign?

In many cases, the answer will not be a single architecture, but a combination of different approaches.

The goal of a BW Diet Strategy is therefore not simply to make the BW system smaller.

It is to ensure that the right workload runs on the right technology, at the appropriate performance level and cost, while creating a gradual path toward SAP Business Data Cloud innovation.
